utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours, and it would be Mr. Tomislav Puhalac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time to deal with some matters. The first is associated exhibit D534 associated to the statement of Stevan Veljovic. During the testimony of Stevan Veljovic document D534 was MFI'd pending a verification of its translation. The Defence has contacted CLSS and received a version of the translation identical to the one already in e-court. The Chamber hereby admits D534 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puhalac. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhalac. Please be seated. Mr. Puhalac, you will first be examined by Mr. Ivetic, you'll find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Can I ask you to please first state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Tomislav Puhalac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to take a look at 1D4400 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, while we have that on the screen this is a written statement from the Karadzic trial. I would like to first ask you if you recall giving this statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is a signature on this page. Can you tell us whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After signing this statement in the Karadzic trial, did you have a chance last week to read the same with me to verify if everything is correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to paragraph 2 of your statement which is to be found on the first page in both versions. In the second paragraph, sir, do you have any corrections in relation to the location names listed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I do. Sokolac should not read Sokoldju [phoen] but Sokolu [phoen] with an L. It should read in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In English it makes no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I note that the Serb states the second location as being Lukavica, whereas the English says Lukavac. Could you please tell us which of these names is correct for the location of the Central National Bureau?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The correct is Lukavica. Lukavac is a different place in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where's the Sokolac in paragraph 2 anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not it's Sokoc in English, S-o-k-o-c, that's the error that's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The fourth line from the bottom of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 6 in English and page 3 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the upper third of paragraph 12 I see here listed an individual who is said to be from Serbia that is reflected as being in the English "Dzindzic," whereas the Serb has the same individual being called "Dzidic," and I'd like to ask you which is the correct identification of the individual brought into the MUP from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what was his ethnicity? Could you tell us what was the ethnicity of this individual with a last name Dzidic from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 8 in the English and page 4 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of paragraph 16, I again see the word Sokoc, S-o-k-o-c, as a place name. Does this also need to be corrected as you've already identified?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, it's Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, apart from these few corrections that we have gone through this morning, do you stand by the rest of your written statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And insofar as you have taken the solemn declaration today, if I were to ask you the same questions today would your answers be the same as in the statement and would they be truthful?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document 1D0440 as the next public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4400 receives number D758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a short summary to read for the public, and it begins as follows. The witness joined the SDB, state security department, of the SRBiH in 1977 and thereafter worked in various functions of that state department. At the outbreak of the war, he was in the department for the prevention of drug abuse. From the beginning of the war until 2005, he worked in the CNB, the Central National Bureau of the Republic of Srpska. Per the witness, the Croat HDZ and Muslim SDA coalition within the BiH MUP did everything they could to discriminate against Serb members and to prevent their involvement in the decision-making process and sensitive work of the SDB and the MUP. This same coalition created a space for the formation of paramilitary units in the MUP, including criminal armed formations. The Muslim state leadership then organised the arming of paramilitary and para-state organs with illegal weapons. The BiH MUP began mobilising and training reserve members who were loyal to the SDA, while notorious criminals were given MUP credentials and these persons began harassing Serb members of the SDB. The witness himself was stopped in Bistrik by heavily armed criminals wearing green berets who took away his official pistol and threatened to kill him in front of his family. When he reported this to the Sarajevo CJB, they refused to undertake any measures. Employment of Serbs in the BiH SDB was discontinued in early April 1992 and they were expelled from Sarajevo, their apartments broken into and plundered, and those that stayed in Sarajevo tortured or killed. And that completes the summary and I'd like to move on now to some additional questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to take a look at paragraph 4 of your statement which will be found on page 1 in the Serb and page 2 in the English versions. Here in this paragraph you identify a Mr. Branko Kvesic, a Croat who became head of the SDB. Did he remain in that position the entire duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, in the beginning of the war he left Sarajevo and together with some other staff he went to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is he Branko or Brane?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is he Branko or Brane?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe he was Branko Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can look at paragraph 7 of your statement which is on page 3 in the English and page 2 in the Serb, here you make reference to "verified information" on the establishment of paramilitary and parastate organisation by the Bosnian Muslim state leadership. Can you be more precise as to what type of verified information you are relying upon here?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: In the period of the end of 1991 and early 1992, I was relying on my personal observations and those of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you, given your position within the Serb national security service, did your service ever have an office or an officer in Trnovo during 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, we did not have an organised section or a representative in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now call up Exhibit P6889 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir -- I'll wait for the English - this document on its face says that it is a report and -- on the activities and operation of the Trnovo SDS municipal board from the period of 01 January to 31st May 1992. Now, first looking at the first page of the report and the header, can you tell us if this follows the standard format for a report that you would expect from your service, your organisation ?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, this is not a document from our service, the one that I worked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at the last page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The report, the one signed, has at the bottom the author listed in the Serbian as Odjeljenje SDB Trnovo. What comment can you make about this formulation of the entity that is stated as being the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: That entity did not exist and this is not a document of any section of the SDB Trnovo. I mean, considering that Trnovo belonged to the Sarajevo centre where I worked, it's not a document from that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What acronym was used for your organisation during 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, beginning with April it was SNB, the national security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, one more thing to note. I read the Serbian title because the English translation has "State Security Service," whereas the Serb original has the acronym "SDB." So I would bring that to Your Honour's attention. I don't know whether we need to have this document revised to have the translation reflect the original or not, but I think it's pretty apparent on the face of the document the acronym. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that the acronym is important because apparently, as the witness told us, the acronym changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you announced this as being an exhibit, but it is a document MFI'd, isn't it, that -- from your --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- questions. I take it that that's what was on your mind when you asked the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That was on my mind. I apologise if I misspoke. I did not have the full notation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document tendered by the Prosecution. You've heard the issue about the translation. Could you please take care that acronym and full text will be verified whether there's any cause of any problem. I do know, however, Mr. Ivetic, that sometimes explanations are not always welcomed by the Defence if it is about translations. But we'll find a solution for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honours. Thank you. I'd like to now go to another document, 65 ter number 1D04409.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when that comes up, sir, my first question to you will be to ask if this is a document that you are familiar with. And now that we have that on the screen that is what I would ask you: Is this a document that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the -- well, let me ask you this way: How is this information in -- or how is this document related to the information contained in paragraph 7 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, it corroborates my assertion because this document came to the headquarters of the service and it was done by my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this individual giving the statement the same person that's identified in paragraph number 7?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've said that your colleagues took the statement. Are you familiar with how the statement was obtained from this individual?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, at the time when he was stopped an interview was made and this information was collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 4 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It appears to be a handwritten version giving the same text in Serbian, and I'd like to ask you: Do you know how the handwritten copy came about in relation to the taking of the statement from this individual?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The person wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "the person," could you please -- are you talking about your colleagues or the individual identified in the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I assume -- actually, I know and I saw it at the time that this draft was handed over. It was done by the person in question, the person that is mentioned in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence at this time as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution objects that there hasn't been adequate foundation laid for this document. If you look at the document itself, it lacks any stamp or official markation and has no signature and the witness's evidence does not lay a sufficient foundation otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 of the witness's statement identifies a confession by a named individual. I have presented it to the witness and he has identified personal knowledge of this document and it being the basis for his evidence in paragraph 7. So I think that the foundation has been established. I -- I mean, the Prosecution is correct that there is no signature and there is no heading, but that doesn't affect the admission of the document. It would go towards weight or other considerations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness's evidence is that he is familiar with the document, that it was done by his colleagues, and that the interview was made and the information was collected. He says that the person wrote it and he saw the document. This is not any information about the making of the document, it's not information about how the interview was conducted, how it was collected. It's -- it's visually seeing the document. It doesn't really provide much more information about the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the admission of this document. Meanwhile, it will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4409 receives number D759, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D759 is marked for identification. Mr. Ivetic, if you introduce again a document like this one, it took me a while to find out what you were talking about because you asked the witness whether he was familiar with it, you apparently are familiar with it, but what it was, it took me at least a couple of minutes to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quickly glancing through it what it was. Therefore, I want to re-read also your questions and the answers when put at the time when I was still figuring out what I was looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honour, I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say maybe we might try to check the translation here because from my limited observation of what's happening here, the handwritten statement says 19th March 1956 - if I'm reading that correctly - the typewritten line says 1953 as the date of birth. So I'm not quite sure whether there may or may not be other mistakes or differences between the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. So perhaps it is best then to submit the handwritten one for translation by CLSS or verification of the translation by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, where does the document originate from? That's often an important --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was an exhibit in the Karadzic proceedings used with this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you serious in saying that you are relying on a -- such an underlying document, a document where you could guess that the Prosecution may have further questions on its origin, and that you say: Well, it's from the Karadzic Defence. You have not verified, you have not asked any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, when it's authenticated from by a witness from the service in two trials, I believe I am justified in relying upon that authentication, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can do whatever you want of course. The only thing I'm saying to you is that if there is a document which, from its appearance and where the witness is not -- well, authenticated, he's -- he says something about it but some of the questions put by Ms. MacGregor, of course, are questions you would expect. And I would have foreseen that rather than to explain that I would rely on what was done in another case. But if you have any further information on it, the Chamber would certainly consider that as well once shared with the Prosecution in its decision on admission or nonadmission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, Your Honours, paragraph 7 of the witness's statement details the taking of this statement. So that is its -- that would be the -- all I can offer at this moment in terms of additional information. If I may proceed, I do have a few other questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just re-reading paragraph 7 to see whether...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I may have a different understanding of what details are. Let's proceed -- but Judge Fluegge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to put a question to the witness. Sir, did you ever meet Senad Memic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who stopped him and conducted an interview with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police forces of the Ilidza police station and the interview was conducted by members of the national security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give me a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. There are names of people who worked there, but I don't know who specifically drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my last category of questions for you will be to ask if your agency had information about the activities of the BiH MUP in forming the Seve unit?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, we had information that such a unit had been formed and was operating illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who, according to your information, in the BiH MUP was behind the formation and operation of the Seve unit?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The AID top officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The transcript does not reflect the organisation. Could you please spell out the acronyms of the organisation just so that we're clear as to who you are referencing.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you identified that they were operating illegally. What sorts of illegal activities was the Seve unit involved in?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: According to our information they were supposed to incite unrest and destabilise the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any specifics of how they were trying to incite unrest and destabilise the situation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: There is one case that I mentioned in my statement, how two members of the unit were killed, attempting to cause unrest in Montenegro. They were killed due to unprofessional handling, and then later their service IDs were found on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And have I exhausted your recollection of other specifics of the activities of the Seve unit?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Information came from a number of sections that the unit was operating, and then later the information was confirmed in some newspaper articles as well as by assertions and the recollection of some persons of Muslim ethnicity who were in Sarajevo at the time. A lot of material on this is being published in the most recent period, and you can read information about this in statements that are given to the press by people in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic, before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness, if the statement, the confession, was made after a truckload of -- or at least a truck with a lot of weapons in it was seized, there must be more material, isn't it, that records the -- this event, I mean apart from an isolated statement and confession? It's -- certainly it could well assist in determining the authenticity and the background of this document if such an event would have been traced, dates known, how much weaponry. That would give a background to this document which would certainly help, perhaps, in better establishing its authenticity. So it's just a suggestion. And I'm also looking at the Prosecution in this respect. It would assist the Chamber if we would know more about the police action taken which resulted in this document. Ms. MacGregor, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am ready. I'm going to bring up my podium. But as I do that, if I can ask the court officer to show the exhibit marked MFI'd as 6889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Puhalac, you'll be cross-examined by Ms. MacGregor. You find her to your right. Ms. MacGregor is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puhalac. I've asked the Court to show again a document that Mr. Ivetic asked you about. You recognise the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have the opportunity to see the document before. If you're thinking about the earlier period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You were shown this document during your preparation for your testimony today by the Defence counsel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Other than counsel showing you this document during that preparation, you've never seen this document before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did not see it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge about the creation of this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I no longer need the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now just for the record, you testified as a Defence witness in the Karadzic trial in March 2013; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And according to your statement, which is now in evidence, you were not a member of any political party during the war but you joined the SDS in 2008; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And not only are you a member, but in November 2012 you were elected as a member -- you were elected to the position of president of the Rogatica municipality for the SDS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, I was not elected as president of the SDS but as the head of the municipality, as a candidate of several parties. Another person was at the head of the SDS. I was just a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What's your current position within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The chief of the or the head of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And still as a member of the SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to briefly turn to your time in Sarajevo at the beginning of the war. Now, you left Sarajevo with your family on April 1st, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: According to your statement at paragraph 15, for the record, that's Exhibit D758, according to that paragraph after the 1st of April you tried on several occasions to return to your MUP office in Sarajevo. Your statement refers to an incident in Vraca where Serb police were fired on when they tried to enter the school of internal affairs building. So that incident you're describing at Vraca, that occurred on April 4th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the Karadzic trial you testified: "After what happened on the 4th of April at Vraca, I stopped trying to go back to the BH MUP ..." Sir, is it correct that as of 4 April 1992, you were no longer in Sarajevo but in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And from that date until the end of the war, you were never back in Bosnian-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And all the evidence that you've provided about events in Sarajevo after the 4th of April is based on information that you received from others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: For the period up to April I'm speaking about personal observations, but from April onwards, since I was working in a service that was based in the eastern part of Sarajevo, in the building of the Energoinvest company to be more precise, I am testifying about assertions and information that came from people who were leaving Sarajevo as well as based on other information such as radio communications and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I please have MFI D759.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm bringing back to the screen the statement of Mr. Memic that you discussed during your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: D759 I believe. Yes. The document -- the correct document that I'm referring to is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, you were not in Sarajevo, as we've just established, on April 14th, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you didn't see Mr. Memic make this statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You don't know where he was when he provided this statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I assume that it was at the Ilidza police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you don't know how long he'd been detained before providing this statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: From what I can remember, he was not in custody. The interview was conducted in agreement between the Serbian and the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When you testified in the Karadzic trial, you did not include knowledge about the handwritten version of this document, which today you claimed was drafted by Mr. Memic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I wasn't asked about it. And now I see the handwritten version ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last portion of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have the handwritten version in front of me at the time, and from what I can remember I think that that is that version in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Today in a response to a question from Judge Fluegge, you stated that you didn't know who drafted the document, the handwritten document -- excuse me, that you didn't know who drafted the document, that's at page 14 of the temporary transcript from today. So you don't know who wrote this document? You don't know based on your own personal knowledge who wrote this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The statement came to the service where I was via our official department. The official department sent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Counsel's question without the Karadzic transcript misstates the Karadzic proceedings, where as transcript page 35097 the question was asked: "Did you see this version in handwriting at the time?" And the answer was: "Yes." So it's incorrect that he did not demonstrate knowledge of a handwritten version existing in the Karadzic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My question was about who had written the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No it was not. It was -- it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- well, could you -- exact line number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll give you the exact line number. It's page 19, line number 24 through 25: "When you testified in the Karadzic trial, you did not include knowledge of the handwritten version of this document..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes. And the last part of the question was at least was ambiguous. Mr. Ivetic, thank you for assisting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, as Mr. Ivetic has pointed out, you did testify that you had seen the handwritten version of this statement and you've just told us today that you were not asked about the handwritten version of the statement when you testified in the Karadzic trial. My underlying question is: Do you have personal knowledge about who wrote the handwritten version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, colleagues from Ilidza sent a statement in written form, and I believe that the statement was written by the man with whom the interview was conducted. In practice it was never the case that something would happen different than what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, could I ask you a question which is -- had you seen this -- who brought this document to your attention during the -- when you were interviewed by the Karadzic Defence? Did you bring it yourself? Or did they present it to you? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They presented it to me, from what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- and you were familiar with that document already when they gave it to you during this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's your recollection from when you saw it for the first time? When did you see it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it was drafted, when it came to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. How did it come to Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By regular mail, regular circulation. We had a section in Ilidza, not just in Ilidza. There were a number of organisational units in the Sarajevo centre area and all the data poured into one point. That's how the service was organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you have a recollection whether -- well, let's say like whether you opened the envelope or whether it was a Sunday? Do you have any recollection about this document, seeing this document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was interesting. That's why I remember. It was notable because of the large quantity of weapons and the way they were obtained. I don't think that I was the one who opened the envelope; that wasn't my job. But we did analyse the document, we reviewed it, so I remember well that it arrived in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the follow-up with Mr. Senad Memic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the interview, as far as I can remember, he went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if a criminal report was issued or not, but this document has to be somewhere in the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you was it common that if someone was arrested carrying weapons in a truck telling during an interview that he had by the thousands delivered such weapons that you would just say after the interview: Thank you very much. Please go home, go to your family. That is -- was that common practice or ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't common practice. But in view of the fact that this was a turbulent, unstable period and that the clashes were just starting, such concessions were made in agreement between the leadership of the sides. So it's my opinion that somebody talked at a higher level or at the top MUP level or at the top political level, and that is why no decision was made to detain the person or hold them further. From what I can remember, probably some important people discussed the issue and the decision was made not to initiate further proceedings as a gesture, as a gesture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but may I ask you to -- not to tell us what you think may have happened but -- and happily enough you are clear on that. But this Chamber is primarily interested in facts rather than in opinions. But I asked you whether it was common and you say under those circumstances such agreements were made. The reason why I'm asking you this is the following: You would be -- you would like to know to whom these weapons were delivered so as to be able to -- well, to do whatever, to limit the damage caused by it. But that -- such follow-up interviews did not take place? If you know; if you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the man was not held for a long time. He was released. And I know it was a gesture of goodwill to avoid deepening the conflict. Every effort was made to avoid conflict and to try to calm the situation down despite such actions. That's a move made by the Serbian side in order to defuse tensions rather than deepen conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said he was not detained for a long time. Do you know when he was arrested and even if not for a long time for how long he was detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. He was brought into custody, if I remember well, for 24 hours maximum. That was the legal limit at the time. That's before the decision was made to hold somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you know exactly the day when he was arrested or the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. If I hadn't seen the date on the document I wouldn't have been able to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but now having seen the date on the document, do you now remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot claim anything with certainty. It would be presumptuous of me to say I remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor -- or Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the time. Maybe we can do this after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had forgotten about the time when I did put questions to the witness which I should not have forgotten about. We take a break. Witness, would you please follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will have missed that information because he had taken his earphones off already but he'll learn about it. We'll take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness I'll briefly deal with another matter which is about D676 MFI'd. During the testimony of Branko Davidovic, document D676 was MFI'd pending an updated translation. Both parties have since agreed upon the updated version of the translation which is Doc ID 1D09-3853, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the updated translation to D676 and admits D676 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge was about to -- Judge Moloto was about to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, when this confession was sent to your office from Sarajevo, did it come under cover of a covering letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you -- did you have sight of that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the practice. Not a single document arrived without a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is it possible to have access to that letter, for the Court to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's possible. It might be in the service. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were not given this when you were given this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because without that covering letter it's not easy to determine where this letter came -- where this document came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm not saying I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not saying you know what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I know it arrived from where I said, but it should have an accompanying document and it did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, this last answer of yours confuses me. You did say yes there was a covering letter; now you say there should have been one, suggesting that you are assuming that there was one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was a cover letter. That was the practice and all the documents arrived with a cover letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, again, Mr. Puhalac, you're telling me of practice. I'm asking you if you did see the letter that accompanied this specific document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you say you don't -- you don't have access to it right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I please have the witness's statement, D758, and if we can look at paragraph 3 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, I've asked the court officer to show you on the screen the statement, paragraph 3 of your statement. I'd like to draw your attention to the following sentence that starts the paragraph. "Considering that I was a member of the State Security Service for many years and was professionally involved in collecting political and security-related information, I can say that I am competent to give you a quality statement regarding events in the Sarajevo-Romanija area that occurred just before the war and at the beginning of the war." In the next paragraph of your statement, paragraph 4, that's on the next page in the English, and also in paragraphs 7 and 11, which I don't need to be displayed on the screen, you give evidence about trafficking of weapons to Muslim forces in Sarajevo in the pre-war period. And you've talked today about the same topic with regard to Mr. Memic's statement. So you must have also known then, given your position at the time in pre-war Sarajevo, that Serbs in Sarajevo were also being armed in that same period, including by the police. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. At that time I lived in Sarajevo and I'm only talking here about things I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I please have document P3792.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm calling up a document that you were shown during your Karadzic testimony. It's a report to the Ministry of Internal Affairs by Tihomir Glavas chief of the public security station in Ilidza, and the report is dated 20 September 1993. Now as we wait for that to come up, you're familiar with Mr. Glavas; is that correct? Sir, do you know who Mr. Glavas is?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I met him during the war. I don't know exactly in which period, but it was when he became commander of the police station at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you're also familiar with Tomo Kovac, commander of the Ilidza police station?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Tomo Kovac I knew before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please have page 2 in both versions of the document, focusing on the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So in this paragraph Mr. Glavas discusses meetings organised by Tomislav Kovac in the beginning of 1991. Reading from the document: "Aside from the obligation that Serbs gather up and prepare for war through these meetings that took place in Dobrinja, Ilidza, and Blazuj, it was also agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality. Armament was transported from Ravna Romanija, Pale, Sokolac, Kalinovik, the village of Nedavici, the village of Tosici, Hadzici, Jusuf Dzonlagic barracks, Lukavica, and Nedzarici" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you've forgotten Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- "and Trnovo."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Puhalac, according to your own words you are competent to give a quality statement about events in pre-war Sarajevo, but do you continue to claim that you had no knowledge in 1991 and into 1992 that Serb police were involved in arming ethnic Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: This looks absolutely unbelievable to me that in 1991 something like this could have been happening. I think somebody was trying to make themselves look important. I don't know to whom this document was sent, but it looks like bragging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked whether you have any knowledge about it. You say "no." There's no need to comment on what may have led the author of this document to write what he wrote. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We can pull the document off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one thing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you couldn't imagine that this happened in 1991. Now, the document also describes events happening in 1992, including distribution of arms to Serbian people. Would you be less surprised that the MUP would have been involved in such activities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people I knew from the MUP, the professional staff of the MUP, I don't know that they ever armed regular citizens or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You have no knowledge about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can please have 65 ter 03838 brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're familiar with Mr. Momcilo Mandic, I assume; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And in March 1992 he held a high position in the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What you see in front of you is a published interview of Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we can please go to the second page in the English and I believe it's -- if we can look in the B/C/S version at the second page too, please. I may need a little help -- third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It's very difficult to see but are you able to see that in front of you, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can have a moment. Because I'm not certain that this is the correct page in the B/C/S, it may be easier if I read from the English unless I can have some input from some of my B/C/S-speaking colleagues. I'm trying to focus here on the end of the first paragraph on the second page in the English, and if you see where it says "in what ways did you help the Serbian side ..." that's the portion I will be asking the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is not the page in B/C/S which is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My limited knowledge left me with that same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be the next page, the left column, about two-fourths -- three-fourths of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ivetic. And Ms. Stewart has shown me the same portion at the bottom left corner. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, if I can draw your attention if you see where it says "in what ways did you help the Serbian side?" Now immediately above that there's the following sentence: "Naturally, I later sided with the Serbs and Serbian movement, helping the Serbian side however I could." And then we see the question: "In what ways did you help the Serbian side? "A. I gave them or put at their disposal official cars, I recruited and admitted to the police force those Serbs proposed by Radovan Karadzic and Rajko Dukic, but I also gave them some material means and communications equipment. We would even deliver weapons to Serbian police stations, for example in Pale, Sokolac, et cetera. We grabbed and shared out as much as was needed." Now, you've testified just now in response to Judge Orie at transcript page 30: "The people I knew from the MUP, the professional staff of the MUP, I don't know that they ever armed regular citizens or anyone else." Now, reading this interview from Mr. Mandic, do you have any further reflections on whether or not you knew that members of the MUP were involved in arming Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: If the question relates to this text by Mr. Mandic, where he's speaking as a Serbian leader and assistant minister who was in charge of supplies of weapons to the police, supplying equipment to the police, for staffing in the police, he's talking about that here. Of course this relates to the weapons that were at the disposal of the MUP. Maybe he was subjective when he talks about the police station in Sokolac and Pale, but this is what it refers to as I read this document you put before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what you think may be the case or what you assume is what may be the case is not what we are primarily interested in. The question was whether reading this interview, whether you have any further reflection on whether you know or do not know that members of the MUP were involved in arming Serbs. And if I understand your answer well the answer is: No, you still, even having read this, do not know anything about that. Is that -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- have we understood you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did want to raise a point. We seem to be mixing apples and oranges. The first question was in relation to arming of civilians and then this document was brought up which does not mention the arming of civilians and yet the generic term "Serbs" was identified for this document, which is why I didn't object because the generic reference to "Serbs" could cover Serb police stations. But I wanted to make clear, given Your Honour's follow-up question, that this document in no way relates to the prior question by Ms. MacGregor as to arming of civilians, at least not the section that has been cited thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: One final question about this document in front of you, Mr. Puhalac. If you see the final question on the English version and the last question on the bottom left-hand corner of the B/C/S version: "When did you start supplying the Serb side, i.e., the SDS? "A. That started around the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992 ..." Would you agree that during that period Mr. Mandic was still part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I no longer need this document and at this time the Prosecution is not tendering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, in your statement you mention a 1991 order by MUP minister Alija Delimustafic to mobilise reserve police forces. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is at paragraph 8 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, in fact at that time ethnic Serbs were also being mobilised, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we can please see 65 ter 16864. While we wait for the document to come to the screen this is a document entitled: "Instructions," it's dated 21 September, 1991, to the SDS municipal boards, and we see Mr. Karadzic's name at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It's a short document and I'm going to read it for the record. "Mobilisation of the war time police force is underway. There are speculations that 100 per cent of the forces are being mobilised, although republic organs can mobilise only 50 per cent. Also, there are speculations that only Muslims are being mobilised or that Serbs are not responding to the mobilisation, which would lead to the creation of Muslim police and to circumstances for a civil war. "I request that you keep an eye on what is going on in regard to the above mentioned. Serbs are to respond to the mobilisation of reserve police. "Inform us on the developments." Is this an example of a mobilisation instruction for Serb members of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. I believe it's authentic and that it was written by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 16864 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16864 receives number P6900, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6900 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your evidence is that Sarajevo in the end of April/beginning of May 1992 was filled with Green Berets armed to the teeth taking over police stations. That's at paragraph 13 of your statement for the record. Now, you were not in Sarajevo at that time, as we've discussed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, from 1 April I was not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And so you must have received this information from interviews of Serbs leaving Sarajevo and other sources; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Which event do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sarajevo was filled with Green Berets armed to the teeth taking over police stations. Did you hear about that from sources that you interviewed and other sources?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, that there were Green Berets around town and that they were armed was obvious to every person in Sarajevo, and I also met them personally at barricades and around the town with the same units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can see paragraph 13 of D758.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, the paragraph I'm talking about specifically refers to the end of April/beginning of May when you weren't there. I'm simply trying to determine where you received the information about that time-period, the information about Green Berets. You can see this statement yourself, paragraph 13 of your statement. From whom did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The information that Pero Petrovic, a policeman, was killed and that the station was taken over by paramilitary units I received from Lazar Bojanic, a man who survived by chance because he was unconscious, they thought him dead. When he left Sarajevo he testified about this. That Juka Prazina took over the police hall next to the police station which was, until then, an institution of the professional police was carried by the media and masses of people who lived in Sarajevo and finally it was shown on Sarajevo TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you also collect information about successful Serb operations in Sarajevo in the time-period of end of April/beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Successful Serb operations? Which ones? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Operations carried out by Serb forces in Sarajevo in the time-period of end of April/beginning of May, did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, we gathered information on all security aspects. Maybe if you asked me a more specific question I could answer. I don't know exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can please have Exhibit 6605.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, this is a published copy of an interview by Miovan Bjelica, president of the Executive Board of the SDS of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a P exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And the B/C/S version is one page and if we can have page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In this interview Mr. Bjelica is asked: "How did you arm the people?" He answers: "Serbian Democratic Party organised all activities related to preparation and organising of people for defence. Since we realised that there had been a great betrayal in the army in former JNA, we had to go to military depots which we assumed would not be in our possession and take weapons from them. The SDS activist played an important role here. First we took the equipment and weapons from western Herzegovina, from Gabela which we brought to Romanija. Then we took the equipment from Central Bosnia from Visoko, from Sarajevo municipalities which were not under our control, and our greatest success was taking the equipment and weapons from Faletic." Mr. Puhalac, Faletici is a weapons depot for Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And Mr. Bjelica continues in response to the next question: "We stole it from their hands. We agreed with then-minister of defence and with a man from security of then Sarajevo Corps." And the next paragraph describes the operation. "We did it by night in April 1992. There was a group of young men, activists of SDS which I was leading ... the first night took whole of artillery and weapons." And I have skipped one portion as I am reading it. "There was about 300 artillery tubes, from 35 to 50.000 rifles as well as other equipment." Skipping again. "Severe attacks on the barracks followed. We were helped by the unit of Colonel Dragoljub Milosevic, i.e., 1st Romanija Brigade, which helped us on the second day ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have to move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry. If we can move to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: "... which helped us on the second day while we were pulling out weapons and equipment. We brought all weapons and equipment to the territory of Romanija in three days." First of all, is that in fact a reference to Dragomir Milosevic that I've just read?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Are you asking me if that's Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, would that be your understanding if you read that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who Mr. Bjelica meant, but if you really want my opinion I believe, yes, that he is thinking of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the factual question is: Witness, do you know any colonel by the name Dragoljub Milosevic or do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragoljub, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Dragomir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met Dragomir Milosevic at the Lukavica barracks. I cannot remember when, but as far as I know he -- there was -- and that was Colonel Milosevic. But it's Dragomir according to my best recollection, not Dragoljub.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So in addition to attacks by Green Berets that you mention in Sarajevo at this time, there were also SDS forces assisted by the JNA lodging attacks in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question where it says assisted by the JNA. The document actually says there was a betrayal on the part of the JNA. The assistance is listed as a minister of defence and with a man from the security organ of the Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Ms. MacGregor you said assisted by the JNA. You relied on what part exactly of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm relying on evidence that's been heard by the Chamber, not specifically to this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- but to this witness I can withdraw the reference to the JNA to keep it simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please put your question again to the witness in the way you would like to do now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the period of late April/early May, were you aware that SDS forces were successfully lodging attacks in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: This is about relocating the Faletici barracks or the weapons depot. I know that the weapons were transferred out of Faletici because the barracks were blockaded and that there was some minor conflicts or clashes that broke out in Faletici. So this is the specific information that I have about that. As for who actually made the transfer, who took part in that, I don't know that, but I do know that the weapons were moved because there was a struggle about who will actually take possession of the weapons, whether it would be the Serb forces or other forces, and I know that the weapons were moved from Faletici. It was an official military weapons depot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Moving away from this document and we can remove it from the screen, Mr. Puhalac, my question is about your knowledge -- not from this document, your knowledge based on sources that you talked to, colleagues that you spoke to, your knowledge about the conditions in Sarajevo in late April/beginning of May 1992. Now, were you aware that during that time-period Serb forces - and I'm referring to the Serb TO, the MUP, the Serb-controlled JNA - that they effected a siege of Sarajevo during that time-period. My question is just: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The barricades were erected on both sides. The ring around Sarajevo was closed by the forces from Sarajevo which set up their own check-points and then the Serb side also placed its check-points facing those. So you could say that Sarajevo was blocked and that check-points were set up by both of the sides, the check-points faced each other. In such a situation where one side was in fear of the other and both feared that clashes would break out, the check-points were set up by each of the sides. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no questions for the witness. I would only thank him again for answering my previous questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no questions for the witness either, this concludes your testimony in this court, Mr. Puhalac. We would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench. You are excused and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement of the witness indeed needs verification. I saw that, for example, the portion read about Juka Prazina taking over a police station that the year is incorrectly stated. The original says "1992, 4th of April"; the translation says "1994." There it should be carefully done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will send -- I will have CLSS notified to take a look at the original and verify it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- those and any other corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will wait for the next witness to enter the courtroom and that would be, Mr. Ivetic -- or Mr. Stojanovic, I see you are ready. Your next witness is ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will be questioning the next witness and the next witness will be Trifko Komad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for him to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may take your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, is it you who will cross-examine Mr. Komad?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll be cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I use the time to deal with another matter which is the redacted witness statement of Witness Ratomir Maksimovic, 65 ter 1D04058a. The Chamber notes that the redacted version of this witness statement of Ratomir Maksimovic has been uploaded into e-court. The unredacted version of the witness's statement, which bears 65 ter number 1D04058, was MFI'd and assigned number D686 during the testimony of the witness. The Chamber would like to know if the Prosecution has any objections to the replacement of the unredacted version of the statement with the redacted version and therefore to the admission of the document bearing 65 ter 1D04058a. If you want to think about it, Ms. Bibles, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll provide an answer after the next break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, just going back to the previous witness, I saw that the last paragraph of his statement was redacted. I don't know whether that was redacted already in the Karadzic case or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was. That's the redaction that was put in place by the Karadzic case based upon a prior objection by the Prosecution in that case and an order from the Chamber in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have -- of course we have no idea what happened in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- no, good morning still, Mr. Komad. Well, the Judges will finalise their struggle on whether 20 minutes to 12.00 is morning or afternoon soon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Komad. Before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Komad. Mr. Komad, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slowly say your correct first and last name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: My name is Trifko Komad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifko, did you at one point provide a statement to the Defence of Radovan Karadzic, a written statement?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at document 65 ter 1D016 -- 1D04474.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all extra microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we understand whether these are two or one document, 1D016 and then 1D04474?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a supplement to the statement that the witness gave to General Mladic's Defence and that is 1D01652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's now a third document you are mentioning, Mr. Stojanovic. You mentioned 1D016 and then 1D044 -- 474. Now you didn't -- been mentioning 1D01652.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I corrected myself because I asked for 1D04474. There is no document that begins with 06, there is no 1D016, and I corrected myself and gave the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, in front of you you can see the statement. I would now like us to look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you look at the last page of the document. Does it -- does this page show a handwritten date and a signature and were these put there by you in your hand?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature and my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we went through the document while we were preparing for your testimony before this Tribunal and today when you gave the solemn declaration, would you still stand by the answers that you gave then to the questions by the Radovan Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by what I said to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender document 65 ter 1D04474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4474 receives number D760, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifko, did you also at one point in time provide a statement to the Mladic Defence, replying to questions that were put to you about your knowledge about specific events that you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 65 ter document 1D01652 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifko, is your signature also on this document that we see now?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the signature and the handwritten date on this page also yours?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While preparing for your testimony, did you tell us that you believed that it would be necessary to supplement your statement with a few words in order for it to be more complete and more clear?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at paragraph 3 of the witness statement, that is 65 ter number 1D01652, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifko, did you feel that it was necessary to add a word in the second sentence of this paragraph after the word "upraising the consciousness of the Serbian people"?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted us to add the word "spiritual consciousness."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would the text of this sentence then read: "The Serbian -- the Serb religious community as well as the development of national consciousness of the Serb people were completely neglected ..." and so on and so forth. So would that be the correct sentence now?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of this statement you indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, what you just read, Mr. Stojanovic, is without the word "spiritual," and I thought that that's what is exactly the word the witness wanted to add, isn't it, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the witness wanted to add the word spiritual, consciousness of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have left it to that then there would have been no confusion. But then you started reading the line as it reads now which was already perfectly clear. And then you left out -- at least in the English translation the word "spiritual" was left out. So it is now in again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
